source.version_note: Invited conceptual article, online7September2025; Analyses of Social Issues and Public Policy25(3):e70031, December2025issue. November2026download stamp does not identify another study.
source.verification_method: All six supplied pages read including bibliography; Figure1 on page4 visually inspected. Main identity/date and Bashkirova reference metadata checked with Crossref. Source summaries compared with earlier completed reviews0019/0033. Selected primary Hofmann abstract/indexed methods passages checked narrowly; no full Hofmann paper, Jost book or other newly cited source was independently read.

citation.title: AI as moral cover: How algorithmic bias exploits psychological mechanisms to perpetuate social inequality
citation.venue: Analyses of Social Issues and Public Policy25(3):e70031

reading.source_scope_note: Invited conceptual integration of motivated reasoning, system justification and moral disengagement, not a new experiment or systematic review. The source explicitly generates/analyzes no dataset. Its examples and mechanism connections are secondary or illustrative, with mixed source types.
access_limits: Complete supplied article, references and conceptual figure read. No new participant/model measurements or fitted mediation model. Only prior reviews0019/0033 document completed original studies cited here.

Primary-source metadata/selected abstract passages support narrow corrections only. Books, library guidance, practitioner blog, other primary studies and intervention effectiveness remain independently unread/unverified.

study.kind: Narrative theoretical synthesis proposing AI as moral cover: psychological filtering and responsibility rationalization may preserve a sense of objectivity while permitting unequal outcomes. No systematic search/inclusion method, prevalence, model comparison, causal test or intervention result.
study.framework: Figure1 links apparently objective AI recommendations→user psychological filters→discriminatory outcomes with maintained legitimacy; dashed arrows are labeled mediation. The selective-adherence, system-justification and moral-disengagement boxes are conceptual explanations, not estimated mediators or proven common causes of every AI discrimination case.
study.motivated_prompting: Illustrates steering a question toward a prejudiced premise. A leading user prompt, system sycophancy, selective acceptance and a feedback loop are distinct potential contributions; none shows the user always acts consciously or that a model has the human’s motive.
study.original_evidence_boundary: Alon-Barkat/Busuioc results reviewed in0033 do not establish blanket AI-specific stereotype adherence: pooled directional Study2 support, nonsignificant source interaction and reversed civil-servant direction matter. Bashkirova/Krpan reviewed in0019 used largely students and fixed mock triage recommendations, with no uniquely correct diagnosis. Those limitations persist when summarized as expert trust.
study.system_justification: Proposes that users defend data-driven outcomes as neutral, legitimate or efficient even when underlying social inequality is reproduced. This is a motivated legitimacy defense, distinct from merely retaining an existing option or presenting a valid moral justification. It can operate without the person explicitly intending discrimination, but the article does not determine intent for a real institution.
study.moral_disengagement: Discusses displacement, diffusion, justification, euphemistic labeling and advantageous comparison. These are secondary theory applications and illustrative language, not separate measured effects. Merely sharing legitimate duties or comparing real alternative harms is not evidence of disengagement.
study.psychological_distance: Suggests delegation creates distance that weakens accountability, and cites fictional/empathetic engagement as another complication. No distance measure, intimacy experiment or causal moderation by anthropomorphism is supplied.
study.institutional_claims: Institutions may accept AI outcomes preserving existing power structures and invoke objectivity when challenged. The claims that this is not hypocrisy or that technical excellence will still perpetuate inequality are explanatory/normative generalizations, not demonstrated universal institutional motives or unavoidable outcomes.
study.interventions: Reflective training, awareness of institutional bias, accountability, careful objectivity claims and context-dependent nondeployment are proposed. Technical fairness/explainability are acknowledged important; the argument does not show them useless or validate a particular training/nondeployment policy.
study.source_mix: Peer-reviewed studies, conceptual books, practitioner commentary and a university library guide play different evidentiary roles. A blog’s yes-man label is not an independent experimental sycophancy study. The article’s six pages are one synthesis, not a new replication of each referenced result.

summary: Add system justification and advantageous comparison with explicit theoretical evidence limits. Enrich existing selective adherence, motivated reasoning, disengagement and responsibility/language mechanisms. Retain moral cover as an integrating framework instead of another overlapping behavior row.

findings.definition: Motivated defense of existing social arrangements or institutions as legitimate, fair or necessary, including arrangements that sustain disadvantage.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Established human theory applied conceptually to algorithmic legitimacy; no new measured system-justification effect or independently completed reading of Jost’s2020book.
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an assistant defends an institutional decision merely because it is current, official or algorithmically produced. Hold evidence fixed, vary institution/beneficiary cues, and assess whether it addresses unequal consequences and alternatives using consistent criteria.
findings.novelty_rationale: The target is legitimacy of a social system, beyond self-favorable reasoning or preference for unchanged options. Moral justification is a broader, potentially valid giving of normative reasons; system justification identifies a motivated defense of the arrangement, which can be unwarranted.

evidence.quote: accept algorithmic discrimination as optimization rather than injustice

findings.evidence_scope: The system-justification section applies Jost’s theory and other secondary work to belief in data-driven neutrality. No scale, manipulated legitimacy threat, causal estimate or demonstrated disadvantaged-group acceptance is supplied.
findings.boundary: Supporting a fair institution or an evidence-based optimization is not bias. Establish the relevant disadvantage and an asymmetric or unsupported legitimacy defense; do not presume every efficiency argument is unjust or every defender knowingly discriminates.

findings.definition: Making harmful conduct seem acceptable or less blameworthy by contrasting it with conduct portrayed as worse.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Secondary moral-disengagement mechanism applied illustratively to AI-versus-human bias; no new experiment or measured mechanism here.
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an assistant excuses a documented harmful action because another actor or system performs worse. Require a relevant, verified alternative comparison and assess remaining rights, duties and feasible remedies rather than treating relative superiority as sufficient justification.
findings.novelty_rationale: Ordinary social comparison concerns evaluating oneself relative to others. This mechanism specifically reduces moral self-censure or scrutiny through a worse comparator. It is a distinct disengagement route rather than all normative justification or all comparison.

evidence.quote: algorithmic bias is better than human bias
AI is framed as the lesser evil.

findings.evidence_scope: The author cites Bandura and gives a conceptual example in which worse human bias is invoked to shield AI from scrutiny/reform. No empirical comparison of the actual alternatives or responsibility change is performed.
findings.boundary: An accurate comparison of feasible harms can legitimately inform a decision. The problem is using a worse comparator to conceal residual wrongdoing, ignore rights or avoid an available remedy; relative improvement alone neither proves nor disproves ethical acceptability.

findings.definition: Preferentially following advice when it matches prior stereotypes or beliefs about the person or group affected by a decision.
findings.novelty_rationale: Central existing mechanism; the synthesis extends institutional interpretation but does not provide a new independent effect.

evidence.quote: following algorithmic advice when it confirms stereotypes

findings.evidence_scope: Narrative interpretation of Alon-Barkat/Busuioc. Original review0033 retains directional-test dependence, null algorithm×name amplification and the reversed civil-servant result. The synthesis’s broad language does not replace those qualifications.
findings.boundary: Advice congruence can reflect relevant knowledge; showing unfair adherence requires matched evidence and applicable criteria. Do not claim universal or uniquely algorithmic amplification from a pooled cue effect.

findings.definition: Marshalling evidence toward a conclusion it prefers or was steered to, rather than following where the evidence leads.
findings.novelty_rationale: Motivated prompting is a task-specific application of this existing process, not a separate behavior entry.

evidence.quote: users frame AI questions in bias-confirming ways
deliberate attempts to use AI for validating prior views

findings.evidence_scope: Illustrative prejudiced prompting and secondary confirmation studies show how the author theorizes user steering. Original0019 measured congruence-related intended acceptance/trust, not diagnostic accuracy or universal expert irrationality.
findings.boundary: A directional prompt can request a legitimate hypothesis test; assess whether assumptions are falsely treated as facts and counterevidence excluded. A user’s inferred motive is not evidence that the model experiences the same motivation.

findings.definition: Suspending moral self-sanctions through justifications that make harmful conduct seem acceptable.
findings.novelty_rationale: The synthesis directly organizes several already-known mechanisms and a newly separated comparison mechanism.

evidence.quote: maintain ethical self-image while enabling discrimination

findings.evidence_scope: Conceptual application of moral-disengagement theory, with illustrative responsibility, efficiency and euphemism claims. No new disengagement scale, observed discrimination experiment or demonstrated mediation.
findings.boundary: Technical opacity, a negative outcome or divided roles does not uniquely identify disengagement. Show the justification/self-sanction process and supported ethical boundary without assuming intent or absence of intent.

findings.definition: Reducing one’s felt responsibility for harmful conduct by assigning responsibility for that conduct to an authority perceived to direct or control it.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source explicitly applies the existing authority-shift mechanism to following data/AI.
findings.evidence_scope: Illustration of attributing a biased result to an algorithm rather than acknowledging one’s role. No measured perceived-authority mediator, assigned blame distribution or observed user motive.
findings.boundary: A tool may genuinely contribute causally without absorbing all human duty. Distinguish evidence-based causal attribution from using perceived instruction to evade an actor’s justified responsibilities.

findings.definition: Diluting felt personal responsibility for harmful conduct by treating responsibility as shared among multiple actors.
findings.novelty_rationale: The article directly distinguishes across-actor spreading from displacement onto an algorithm.

evidence.quote: each participant feels less responsible for its failures

findings.evidence_scope: Theoretical statement about developers, managers and end users, not an observed universal consequence of partial control or a measured accountability decline.
findings.boundary: Multiple actors can each have substantial legitimate duties; a many-hands structure is not sufficient evidence of diffusion or nobody accountable. Compare felt duty with justified roles and actual control.

findings.definition: Language that makes the bad seem neutral or positive.
findings.novelty_rationale: Euphemistic labeling is the same existing language mechanism; do not create a synonym row.

evidence.quote: Discrimination becomes “model variance,” and inequality becomes “predictive limitation.”

findings.evidence_scope: Illustrative relabeling of harm in technical language, not measured language frequency or a claim every use of these terms conceals discrimination.
findings.boundary: Technical terms can accurately describe real properties. Establish what material harm is obscured and whether terminology changes understanding/accountability, rather than banning a neutral phrase.

findings.definition: Obscuring a human actor’s role in morally suspect actions by attributing those actions to an algorithm, machine or technical system.
findings.novelty_rationale: Institutional moral cover overlaps the existing accountability-obscuring process; the multi-mechanism framework is retained in the review rather than added as a duplicate.

evidence.quote: institutions may use AI to protect themselves from moral scrutiny
they point to the technology as objective proof

findings.evidence_scope: Conceptual institutional account linking selective acceptance, legitimacy and disengagement. No observed intent, institution-level causal mechanism or frequency is established. The author’s claim that this is not hypocrisy is not generalized to all cases.
findings.boundary: Identifying genuine model contributions is legitimate; laundering requires obscuring a relevant human role or duty. It may involve conscious or unrecognized rationalization, and case-specific evidence is needed rather than assuming either.

source_corrections.issue: The synthesis presents Alon-Barkat/Busuioc as straightforward support for users following AI stereotypes and dismissing counterstereotypes.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Completed original review0033 shows mixed evidence: Study2 pooled name-cue OR1.50,two-sidedp.083/preregistered directionalp.042; nonsignificant algorithm×name interaction; reversed civil-servant effect. Preserve the selective-adherence hypothesis without claiming replicated AI-specific amplification.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Previously fully read original supplied paper; not a fresh replication or a new full version comparison.

source_corrections.issue: Experts/mental-health-professionals phrasing obscures the predominantly student sample, and bibliography lists volume3.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Original review0019:114eligible participants included92students and only two practicing clinical psychologists; intended acceptance/trust of fixed mock recommendations, no uniquely correct diagnosis. Crossref gives Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans2(1):100066,2024,DOI10.1016/j.chbah.2024.100066,not volume3.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Earlier full read plus current identity/locator metadata check; not evidence that congruence necessarily produces diagnostic mistakes.

source_corrections.issue: More covert racial bias than any human stereotype ever recorded drops the racial-target, task and historical-comparison scope.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: The cited work concerns dialect prejudice toward African American English speakers, compared with specific historical human stereotypes about African Americans in Princeton Trilogy studies. Do not broaden this to every form of racial bias, every human stereotype, every language/model or a common numeric racism scale across all settings. The primary abstract itself uses strong language; the scope must remain visible.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Selected primary abstract/indexed comparator-method passages only. Nature direct fetch was access-blocked; full original paper and all historical datasets not read. No replacement numerical result is asserted.

methodological_limits: One conceptual integration is not independent experimental confirmation of every cited mechanism, and its figure arrows do not estimate mediation or causal magnitudes.
Individual reasoning, institutional legitimacy, actual algorithm unfairness and legal discrimination differ; no single framework establishes every level simultaneously.
The source’s assertion that technical approaches ignore psychology is a broad framing, not a systematic finding that the entire fairness literature omits human factors.
Non-intentional harm, dehumanization and efficient goal pursuit are not interchangeable; neither malicious intent nor its absence is established for all institutions.
The proposed training/reflection and nondeployment approaches are untested here. Technical and human mitigations may be complementary.

A neutral output can be unfair and an unfavorable output justified; substantiate the affected groups, relevant criteria, alternative decisions and actual harms rather than infer bias from rhetoric alone.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Selective-adherence evidence is conditional/mixed, with a reversed civil-servant cue effect and no significant AI-specific amplification. Later theoretical syntheses must preserve those original limitations.
Expert congruence preferences need participant composition and diagnostic ground-truth limits. Congruence is not itself proof that rejecting advice was wrong.

Both argue technical debiasing may be insufficient without context, scrutiny and human practices. This synthesis emphasizes legitimacy/self-regulation; DAB adds system dependence/control. Neither validates a mitigation intervention.

Organizational-benefit messages and responsibility interpretations are relevant, but hypothetical intentions and inferred disengagement do not establish actual misconduct or a causal moral-cover pathway.
Normative shared responsibility can support answerability rather than weaken it; many hands and psychological diffusion must not be collapsed.

deferred.reason: Integrating label spanning selective adherence, system justification, disengagement and agency laundering. Preserve its framework links without inflating the list with a composite synonym.
Context-specific manifestations of motivated reasoning and sycophancy already represented; practitioner/library guidance is not a new behavioral experiment.
Brief secondary account conflates unintended harm/goal pursuit with dehumanization. Read the cited original conceptual paper before deciding a distinct operational boundary.
Secondary leads; this synthesis does not independently test intimacy, feedback dynamics or their causal relation to discrimination. Retain cited-original leads without adding unverified effects.

limitations: Jost’s2020book, Bandura’s original, referenced blogs/library guidance and other full cited works are not newly completed readings. One synthesis can be a relevant conceptual citation but not a replication. No automatic ethical/harm edges or fabricated annual mention totals.
